title: Vishwakarma Jayanti: India's own Labour Day
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Why BMS observes 17 September as National Labour Day: who Vishwakarma is, the May Day argument on both sides, and how the day is observed.
body:
Every year, on **17 September**, BMS and its units observe **Vishwakarma Jayanti** as **National Labour Day**. Workshops and factories are cleaned, tools are worshipped, and many places hold cultural programmes. For BMS this is not a side event. It is a statement about what a day for workers should mean. This post sets out who Vishwakarma is, why BMS prefers this day to 1 May, what the argument looks like on both sides, and how the day is observed.

## Who is Vishwakarma?

In Hindu tradition **Vishwakarma** is the divine craftsman, the architect of the gods. Wikipedia notes that in the early texts this role belonged to Tvashtar, and that the name Vishvakarman first appears as an epithet for a powerful deity, in the tenth book of the Rigveda. Later texts credit him with building the chariots and weapons of the gods and with cities such as Lanka, Dvaraka and Indraprastha. The Brahmavaivarta Purana links him with many artisan groups, among them carpenters, ironsmiths, goldsmiths, stonemasons, weavers and potters.

BMS-aligned writers draw particular attention to the Rigveda hymns numbered 10.81 and 10.121, in which Vishwakarma is presented as the creator, and they call him the first labourer and the teacher of labour. In this reading the point is not a particular legend. It is that Indian tradition honours work as something close to worship, and that the skilled worker is a respected figure.

## Why not May Day?

The argument is made at length in an Organiser article of 1 May 2023 by C. K. Saji Narayanan, then BMS's National President. The article is an opinion piece that sets out BMS's position, and it makes historical claims that readers should check for themselves. Its main points, paraphrased, are these.

- May Day is a Western import. It commemorates the agitation for an eight-hour working day in Chicago in 1886, and in BMS's view it came to be associated with class conflict and with Communist politics.
- Vishwakarma Jayanti offers a homegrown symbol for the dignity of labour, which the article says would motivate workers more positively.
- To give the observance a common date across the country, BMS fixed it on 17 September. Traditionally the day is marked in some places on Bhadrapada Shukla Panchami and in others on Magha Shukla Trayodashi, so the fixed date is a convention.
- The article says that several States have officially declared Vishwakarma Jayanti as Labour Day, but it does not name them, and we have not independently checked which.

## The history of May Day, in brief

Supporters of May Day, and historians, tell the story in a different way. According to Wikipedia, a general strike for the eight-hour day began in the United States on 1 May 1886. On 4 May, in Haymarket Square in Chicago, police moved to disperse a rally and a bomb was thrown. Police fired, and seven officers and at least four civilians died. Four labour leaders were later hanged after a trial that the article calls a miscarriage of justice. In 1889 the International Workers Congress in Paris, which established the Second International, called for a great international demonstration for the eight-hour day, and May Day spread from there.

The BMS article reads this history differently. It argues that the 1 May strike itself was peaceful, that the violence occurred on 3 and 4 May, and that the American labour movement itself later chose the first Monday of September for its Labour Day. On that last point, Wikipedia confirms that Labor Day in the United States falls on the first Monday of September and became a federal holiday in 1894, after the Pullman Strike. BMS's further claims about the Communist movement's use of the day between 1929 and 1940 are the author's argument, and we do not endorse or dispute them here.

What is fair to say is that May Day is observed as International Workers' Day in a large number of countries. Wikipedia's infobox lists 95. It is also true that, in India, it has been the day on which many unions of different political colours have held their rallies.

## What the debate is really about

It is not a dispute about whether workers should be celebrated. Everyone in the labour movement agrees on that. It is about what the celebration should say. BMS's position is that labour is a **creative, sacred and national** act, and that the relationship between worker and employer should be pictured as that of members of one industrial family and not as a war between classes. The BMS slogans quoted in the article, such as work is worship, express this view. Its critics answer that the dignity of workers has often had to be won against employers, that conflict is real in many workplaces and that a day of struggle reminds people of the cost of past gains.

Both sides, in other words, are arguing about the character of the labour movement itself. That is a debate worth having openly, and it is better conducted with accurate history than with slogans.

## How Vishwakarma Puja is observed

Outside BMS, Vishwakarma Puja is widely observed by workers in factories and workshops. Wikipedia says it falls around 16 to 18 September, on Kanya Sankranti, that 17 September is in many places a restricted holiday, and that in Nepal it is a full holiday. Tools and machines are venerated at the workplace, and prayers are offered for safe working conditions and for the smooth operation of machinery.

An IANS report on Bengal describes what this looks like on the ground. Artisans, mechanics, welders, masons and factory workers honour Vishwakarma. Pujas are held in nearly every locality, including bus terminals and rickshaw stands. Factories and warehouses close, idols are installed at factories and workshops, vehicles are garlanded, and workers share a feast. Young people fly colourful kites, and kite-flying contests are held in many localities. It is an occasion that belongs to a large part of working India regardless of union affiliation.

Within BMS, the observance usually includes:

- flag hoisting at BMS offices and unions;
- puja of tools and machines;
- felicitation of senior workers; and
- blood donation, health camps and other social service.

The day has also been used as an occasion by the Government. The PM Vishwakarma Scheme for traditional artisans was launched on 17 September 2023, as the previous post in this series describes.

## Both can be true

Many Indian workers observe both days, marching on 1 May and worshipping their tools on 17 September, and see no contradiction. What BMS asks is that the Indian tradition gets its due: that the country's labour festival should speak in an idiom that its workers recognise. Whether one chooses May Day, Vishwakarma Jayanti or both, the substance of the day is what happens after it. Safe workplaces, fair wages and a seat at the table are the measures by which any Labour Day should be judged.

The new India that we hope for includes a Labour Day with its own roots, and a workforce that is honoured on every other day of the year as well.
